post.name: Dante audio networking, explained
post.excerpt: Dante sends multichannel audio over standard networks. Here's why it simplifies event and install audio.
post.body:
Short answer: Dante carries many channels of digital audio over a standard Ethernet network. One network cable can replace a heavy analog snake, and routing is changed in software.

How it works

Each Dante device, whether a mixer, stage box, amplifier or wireless receiver, appears on the network. A controller app shows every output and input as a grid, and you click to connect them.

Why crews like it

  • One Cat6 run instead of dozens of copper pairs
  • Latency low enough for live sound
  • Add a recording feed or overflow space without new cable
  • Redundant primary and secondary networks for critical shows

Where it fits

Corporate events, venues with several spaces and permanent installs, anywhere sources and speakers are spread out. For one small space, analog is still fine.

What the network needs

  • Managed gigabit switches with energy-saving modes turned off
  • A dedicated VLAN for audio
  • Quality of service set for clock and audio packets
  • No WiFi in the audio path

Common mistakes

  • Running Dante on the guest network
  • Mixed sample rates between devices
  • No secondary network on a show that cannot stop

The bottom line

Dante is reliable when the network is designed for it. Treat the switch like part of the sound system, because it is. See our audio service.

industry.h1: Trade show booth AV, built for the show floor.
industry.sub: Booths that stand out on the floor and stay online when the hall network does not. Built and taken down on the show's schedule.
industry.challenge: Show floors are hard on equipment: tight build windows, fast teardown and a hall full of competing screens.
industry.offer:
• Displays, audio and interactive pieces for the booth
  • Booth structures and fixtures from our shop
  • A network of our own, so demos stay online
  • A technician on the floor for opening, on call after
industry.scope: Booth display, demo station, show-floor activation.
industry.faq:
What do you handle in a booth?

The whole AV side: displays, audio and interactive pieces, plus fixtures from our shop, planned as one system.

Can you work to the show's build and teardown windows?

Yes. The booth is built and tested in Brooklyn first, so the time on the floor goes into placing and checking.

Is someone on site during the show?

Yes. A technician is on the floor for opening and on call for the rest of the show.

Can you add an LED wall to the booth?

Yes. LED walls go through our sister site ledwall.nyc, and we plan them in with the rest of the booth.

How do we start?

Send us the show, the booth size and what the booth has to do. We reply within 24 hours.
